analytic.title: Worst case response time analysis of sporadic task graphs with EDF non-preemptive scheduling on a uniprocessor

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper considers the problem of non-preemptive hard realtime scheduling of sporadic task graphs on a uniprocessor with Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling. A sporadic task graph associated to an application is characterized by a set of subtasks under precedence constraints with deadline constraints. We study feasibility conditions based on the computation of the worst case response times of any subtask of a task graph. We investigate the late deadline constraint.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: We consider in this paper the problem of hard real-time scheduling of sporadic task graphs with Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling. A task graph is composed of a set of subtasks with precedence constraints. We establish feasibility conditions to ensure that every subtask of a graph respects timeliness constraints. The timeliness constraints investigated in this paper are late deadlines imposed on the worst case response time of every subtask. The worst-case response time (WCRT) of any subtask in a task graph depends on the precedence constraints of the subtasks and on the scheduling chosen to schedule the subtasks with no precedence constraints (EDF in this paper).

Real-time scheduling has been extensively studied in the last thirty years. Feasibility conditions for the independent nonpreemptive sporadic task scheduled EDF was introduced by [2], [1] and [4]. In 1973, [7] presented an optimal algorithm that minimizes the maximum lateness of a set of tasks with precedence relations and simultaneous arrival times. [9], [10] solved the problem of scheduling tasks with precedence constraints by changing their relative deadlines. The feasibility analysis for sporadic task graphs and preemptive fixed priority scheduling was proposed by [3], [12]. The solution is based on a graph transformation into a chain. The chain is used to establish the response time of a task graph. This approach was further developed by [5] in the case of re-entrant graph for mixed preemptive and non preemptive subtasks with fixed priority scheduling.

We consider in this paper non re-entrant task graphs. We show how to transform a task graph into a chain and study the worst case response time of a subtask in its chain. The scheduling of independent subtasks is EDF. EDF scheduling is interesting as it has been shown to be optimal for the scheduling of independent preemptive ( [13]) and non-preemptive ( [1]) sporadic tasks when tasks first arrival times are not known a priori. EDF is therefore an interesting algorithm to consider for scheduling subtasks of a graph task with no precedence relations. Furthermore, for subtask run in the kernel space, the scheduling used is generally nonpreemptive. We first define the concepts and notations in section 2. We describe the sporadic graph model and show how to transform a graph into a chain, easier to analyse. In section 3, we propose a feasibility condition for non-preemptive EDF task graph scheduling. We illustrate the feasibility conditions by an example in section 4. Finally, we conclude.

div.head: Notations
div.p: In this paper, we consider a set τ = {τ 1 ,…,τ n } of n sporadic task graphs. A Sporadic task graph τ i , is defined by: • G i : a graph of subtasks with precedence constraints, • T i : the minimum inter-arrival time, called the period of the task graph By definition, G i (τ i )={τ i 1 ,…τ i ni } is the set of n i subtasks composing the graph G i . Notice that a subtask can not be preempted. A partial order is defined for the subtasks, the order specifying operation precedence constraints.

By definition, the absolute deadline of a subtask τ i j corresponding to a graph task τ i requested at time t i is t i + D i j .
We consider the following scheduling:
• Subtasks with precedence relations are scheduled according to their precedence relations, whatever their deadlines.

Subtasks with no precedence realations are scheduled according to non-preemptive Earliest Deadline First (EDF). EDF schedules the subtasks according to their absolute deadlines: the subtask with the shortest absolute deadline has the highest priority. Ties are broken arbitrarily.
A task graph G i for a task τ i , requested at time t i results in the activation of all its subtasks. Hence, for any subtask τ i j of G i , its absolute deadline is t i + D i j .

div.p: Furthermore, we assume that: • Time is discrete (task arrival times and task executions begin and terminate at clock ticks; the parameters used are expressed as multiples of the clock tick); in [6], it is shown that there is no loss of generality with respect to feasibility results restricting the schedules to being discrete, once the task parameters are assumed to be integers (multiples of the clock tick).
An idle time t is defined on a processor as a time, such that there are no subtasks released before time t pending at time t. An interval of successive idle times is called an idle period.
• A busy period is defined as a time interval [a,b), such that there is no idle time in [a,b) (the processor is fully busy) and such that both a and b are idle times.

Given a non-concrete graph task set, the synchronous busy period is defined as the time interval [0,L) delimited by two successive idle times in the scenario where all tasks are released at the same time [11]. The value of L does not depend on the scheduling algorithm, as far as it is non-idling, but only on the task arrival pattern. L is called the length of the synchronous busy period. The value of L is given is section 3.1.

div.head: Graph to chain transformation
div.p: We now show how to transform a graph into a chain, easier to analyse. We show that this does not change the feasibility results. We then compute the response time of any subtask in a chain.
The following procedure 1 describes how can transform a graph G i of a task τ i into a chain:
Procedure 1:
1. Set chain to empty.

div.head: Consider all the subtasks in the graph having no predecessor. Select among these subtasks the subtask, which has the minimum relative deadline, insert it at the end of the current chain and remove it from the graph 3. Proceed to point 2 until the graph is empty
Procedure 1: Graph to chain transformation
div.p: After the transformation, the subtasks are indexed by increasing index from τ i 1 , the first subtask to execute, to τ i ni where n i is the number of subtasks of the graph task τ i . In the following sections, τ i j therefore represents the j th subtask in the chain obtained from graph G i . The following lemma proves that this transformation does not change the schedulability problem.

Lemma 1: Scheduling the subtasks according to their chain obtained using procedure 1 does not change the scheduling order obtained for of the subtasks when scheduled according to their graph. Proof : Let ϒ* be the processing order of subtasks of graph G i and ϒ be the scheduling order obtained from the chain of G i . Consider two successive subtasks τ i j and τ i k in ϒ*. We have two cases: (i) the subtasks have precedence constraints between them (ii) the subtasks have no precedence constraints between them. In the first case, as the chain is built from the precedence constraints, the execution order of τ i j and τ i k is the same in ϒ. In the second case, EDF scheduling is used to arbitrate between τ i j and τ i k . As all the subtasks of a graph are released at the same time (see section 2.1), the absolute deadline used by EDF for subtasks in a graph and subtasks in a chain are the same. Leading to the same processing order equal to ϒ, from procedure 1.

We now transform the chain into its canonical form w.r.t a subtask τ i j . This transformation is required for the response time computation. This modification consists in changing the relative deadline of a subtask τ i m-1 to the relative deadline of τ i m if its relative deadline is smaller than τ i m , starting from m=j down to m=2. This allows obtaining a set of consecutive subtasks with equal or decreasing relative deadlines from τ I 1 to τ i j . The relative deadlines of the subtasks after τ i j are left unchanged.
The following lemma proves that the completion time of the subtask τ i j in the chain of G i and the completion time of τ i j* in its canonical chain are the same.

div.head: Lemma 2 :
div.p: The completion time of any subtask in a chain of Gi is unchanged considering the same subtasks in its canonical chain. Proof: Consider two consecutive subtasks τ i j and τ i j+1 in the chain of G i . We have two cases: (i) D i j > D i j+1 and (ii) D i j D i j+1 . In the first case, by construction the canonical chain will preserve the relative deadlines of the subtasks τ i j and τ i j+1 . In the second case with the canonical transformation, we obtain D i j* = D i j+1 and D i j+1 is unchanged. The subtasks scheduled between the absolute deadline of τ i j and τ i k will be scheduled before τ i j but not after τ i k thus leaving unchanged the starting time of τ i k . As subtasks following τ i j+1 are unchanged, the completion time of τ i j is also unchanged.

div.head: non-preemptive subtasks
div.p: Owing to the absence of preemption, a subtask instance with later absolute deadline can possibly cause a priority inversion, which must be accounted for. Always owing to the non-preemptability of any subtask instance execution, our attention will be on the busy period preceding the execution start time of the instance, and not on the busy period preceding its completion time, as in the case in the preemptive model. div.head: CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we have studied the problem of scheduling sporadic task graphs with non-preemptive EDF scheduling. We have proposed a feasibility condition to ensure that any subtask of a task graph meets late deadlines. The feasibility conditions are based on the computation of worst case response time of each subtask of a task graph with the non-preemptive EDF scheduling.
